text: Everything in this path so far has run on CPUs — web apps, APIs, data platforms. AI training and inference are different, and understanding why starts with the hardware itself. This lesson is about what a GPU actually is at the architecture level, and why that architecture happens to be a near-perfect match for the math behind neural networks.

A modern CPU has somewhere between four and a hundred and twenty eight cores, each genuinely sophisticated — deep pipelines, branch prediction, large caches, built to finish one instruction stream as fast as possible. A GPU throws that out. An NVIDIA A100 packs almost seven thousand simpler cores, with the goal flipped: not finish one thing fast, but run the same operation across huge amounts of data at once. Few expert chefs, versus a kitchen with thousands of line cooks who can all chop at the same time.

Here's the fact that makes GPUs the default for AI: training and running a neural network is, arithmetically, overwhelmingly matrix multiplication. A dense layer's forward pass multiplies weights against activations. Backward passes compute gradients the same way. Convolutions reshape into matrix multiplies. Transformer attention — the mechanism behind every modern language model — is built entirely from matmuls: scoring query against key, then applying that weighted sum against value. The operation dominating AI compute cost is exactly what GPU hardware was built to accelerate.

GPU cores execute in groups called warps, thirty-two threads at a time, all running the same instruction simultaneously — SIMT, single instruction, multiple threads. When a matmul's inner loop is just 'multiply two numbers and add to an accumulator,' you issue that instruction across thousands of threads at once. CPUs have a vector equivalent, but with eight or sixteen lanes, not thousands — that gap in parallel lane count is the real source of the speedup, far more than raw clock speed.

Since the Volta architecture, NVIDIA GPUs add Tensor Cores: circuits built to perform a small matrix multiply-accumulate in one operation, usually at reduced precision like FP16 or BF16. That's not just more cores — it's a specialized circuit tuned for the pattern that dominates deep learning math. It's also why mixed-precision training is standard: compute in FP16 for speed, accumulate in FP32 so results stay stable. Azure's NC-series and AWS's P-series are both built around GPUs with this exact capability.

So that's the core idea: thousands of simple, parallel cores plus specialized Tensor Circuits, matched almost perfectly to matrix-multiplication-heavy math. Compute speed is only half the story, though. Next lesson tackles the constraint that actually fails training jobs most often in practice — GPU memory, and why running out of it is far more common than running out of raw compute.
